examGuide.title: Mental model and derivation
examGuide.body:
Conflicts involve the same data item, different transactions and at least one write. A precedence graph orders transactions by conflicting operation order. It is acyclic exactly when a schedule is conflict-serializable; topological orders give equivalent serial schedules. Read-read pairs and accesses to different items do not add edges. View serializability is broader, so graph cycles refute conflict serializability, not every possible equivalence notion.

**Key relationship:** Conflict-serializable ⇔ precedence graph is acyclic

examGuide.title: A repeatable solving procedure
examGuide.body:
1. Enumerate conflicting pairs.
2. Add directed edges in schedule order.
3. Find cycles or topological serial orders.

examGuide.title: Approach the exam question
examGuide.body: Build a precedence graph from conflicting same-item operations in different transactions, preserving their order. Read-read pairs create no edge. Acyclicity is equivalent to conflict serializability; any topological order is a valid equivalent serial order. Commit order alone does not determine the graph.

examGuide.title: Worked problem
examGuide.body:
Schedule r1(X), w2(X), w1(Y), r2(Y) involves two transactions. How many directed edges occur in its precedence graph?

**Answer: 1.** r1(X) before w2(X) gives T1→T2. w1(Y) before r2(Y) gives the same edge, not a second distinct graph edge. There is one edge, and the schedule is conflict-equivalent to T1 then T2.

examGuide.title: Conditions and edge cases
examGuide.body:
Multiple operation conflicts can support the same edge. A cycle requires opposite dependencies or a longer directed loop, not repeated copies of one edge.

A cycle proves failure of conflict serializability, not every possible definition of serializability.

examGuide.title: Worked question patterns
examGuide.body:
#### Pattern 1 · MCQ

Which pair conflicts across different transactions?

- **A.** R₁(A),W₂(A)
- **B.** R₁(A),W₂(B) for A≠B
- **C.** Reads of unrelated items
- **D.** R₁(A),R₂(A)

**Answer: A.** A read/write pair on the same item conflicts. Read/read and different-item operations do not.

#### Pattern 2 · MSQ

Choose true statements.

- **A.** Acyclic precedence graph implies conflict serializability
- **B.** Every serial order respects any precedence graph
- **C.** All read-read pairs add edges
- **D.** A cycle disproves conflict serializability

**Answer: A, D.** Acyclic graphs permit topological serial orders, but arbitrary orders may violate edges. Read-read pairs add no edge, and cycles refute conflict serializability.

#### Pattern 3 · NAT

A precedence graph has T1→T2 and T1→T3 only. Number of serial topological orders?



**Answer: 2.** T1 must be first. T2 and T3 can follow in either order: two serial orders.

examGuide.title: Work through the supplied PYQs
examGuide.body:
#### GATE 2024 CS1 · Q46 · MSQ

[Open the original question and try it](/#/lesson/serializability?tab=practice)

**What is tested:** Conflict serializability. Refer to the original image for complete givens and diagrams.

1. T1 accesses only z, while T2 and T3 access x,y. There are no intertransaction conflicts involving T1.
2. On y, T3’s read/write precedes T2’s read/write, giving the sole precedence constraint T3→T2.
3. Any serial ordering that places T3 before T2 is conflict-equivalent: **T1 T3 T2, T3 T2 T1, T3 T1 T2**, options **B,C,D**. A reverses that conflict.

#### GATE 2026 CS2 · Q20 · MCQ

[Open the original question and try it](/#/lesson/serializability?tab=practice)

**What is tested:** Conflict serializability. Refer to the original image for complete givens and diagrams.

1. Operations by different transactions on the same item conflict if at least one operation writes that item.
2. Two reads commute and do not change the shared value, so a read–read pair is nonconflicting. Read–write, write–read and write–write pairs all conflict.
3. The required condition is **both only read A, A**.
